title: HMS Bounty: Tahiti, the Mutiny and the Two Ways Home
intro: HMS Bounty left England in 1787 to collect breadfruit plants in Tahiti for the British colonies in the West Indies, under Lieutenant William Bligh. On 28 April 1789 acting-Lieutenant Fletcher Christian and others seized the ship and set Bligh and 18 loyalists adrift in the launch. The journey then divides: Bligh's open-boat voyage to Timor, and the mutineers' search for a refuge.
ending: Bligh and his men reached Kupang on 14 June 1789 and Bligh landed in England on 14 March 1790. Christian's party settled on Pitcairn Island, where several mutineers and all six Tahitian men died in violence by 1794; the community was found by an American sealer in February 1808.

stops.text: Bounty had been refitted at Deptford Dockyard under Joseph Banks's supervision, its great cabin turned into a greenhouse for over a thousand breadfruit plants. It left Deptford for Spithead to await final sailing orders.
stops.quote: On 15 October 1787, Bounty left Deptford for Spithead, in the English Channel, to await final sailing orders.

stops.text: The Admiralty delayed Bligh's orders for three weeks. Bounty sailed on 28 November but was held by contrary winds and could not clear Spithead until 23 December.
stops.quote: When Bounty finally sailed on 28 November, the ship was trapped by contrary winds and unable to clear Spithead until 23 December.

stops.text: Stormy weather off Cape Horn had driven Bounty back, and on 17 April Bligh turned for the Cape of Good Hope. The ship anchored in False Bay, where five weeks went on repairs and provisions.
stops.quote: On 24 May 1788, Bounty anchored in False Bay, east of the Cape of Good Hope, where five weeks were spent in repairs and reprovisioning.

stops.text: Bligh sighted Mewstone Rock on 19 August and anchored in Adventure Bay two days later. The crew rested, fished, filled water casks and felled timber, with peaceful encounters with the native population.
stops.quote: Bligh's skill was such that on 19 August he sighted Mewstone Rock, on the south-west corner of Van Diemen's Land and, two days later, made anchorage in Adventure Bay.

stops.text: Bounty anchored after a journey of 27,086 nautical miles. Over five months many of the men lived ashore, Christian formed a close relationship with a Polynesian woman named Mauatua, and Bligh's punishments grew harsher.
stops.quote: Bounty came to anchor in Matavai Bay, Tahiti, on 26 October 1788, concluding a journey of 27,086 nautical miles (50,163 km; 31,170 mi).

stops.text: Bounty left Tahiti on 5 April with the breadfruit plants. At Nomuka Christian led a watering party that Bligh had ordered to leave its arms in the boat, and Bligh cursed him when the party returned with the task incomplete.
stops.quote: On 22 April 1789, Bounty arrived at Nomuka, in the Friendly Islands (now called Tonga), intending to pick up wood, water and further supplies on the final scheduled stop before the Endeavour Strait.

stops.text: Early in the morning Christian, with the help of men he had approached, took the ship and had Bligh tied and brought to the quarterdeck. Bligh and 18 loyalists were put into the launch, which was left with seven inches of freeboard.
stops.quote: In the early hours of 28 April 1789, Bounty lay about 30 nautical miles (56 km; 35 mi) south of the island of Tofua.

stops.text: Bligh hoped to find water and food ashore. The people of Tofua grew menacing, and on 2 May they seized the launch's stern rope. The quartermaster John Norton leapt into the water and was stoned to death.
stops.quote: On 2 May, four days after landing, Bligh realised that an attack was imminent.

stops.text: Having decided to sail for Kupang, the launch passed through the Fiji Islands without stopping, for fear of cannibalism. On 28 May Bligh found a gap in the Great Barrier Reef and landed on an island he named Restoration Island, where the men ate oysters and berries.
stops.quote: On 28 May, the Great Barrier Reef was sighted; Bligh found a navigable gap and sailed the launch into a calm lagoon.

stops.text: The launch cleared the northern point of the Australian continent and steered through shoals and reefs. That evening it reached the Arafura Sea, still 1,100 nautical miles from Kupang.
stops.quote: On 2 June, the launch cleared Cape York, the extreme northern point of the Australian continent.

stops.text: The coast of Timor was sighted on 12 June, and the launch sailed into Kupang harbour under a makeshift Union Jack after about 3,500 nautical miles. Bligh reported the mutiny, and the botanist Nelson soon died of the climate.
stops.quote: On 14 June, with a makeshift Union Jack hoisted, they sailed into Kupang harbour.

legs.title: Christian's way: Tubuai, Tahiti and Pitcairn

stops.text: Christian threw the breadfruit plants into the sea and made for Tubuai, which he thought easy to defend. The islanders were hostile, and when war canoes came towards the ship Christian fired a four-pounder gun, killing at least a dozen warriors.
stops.quote: Bounty arrived at Tubuai on 28 May 1789.

stops.text: To settle on Tubuai the mutineers needed labour and women. Christian told the Tahitian chiefs a false story that he, Bligh and Cook were founding a settlement at Aitutaki, and on 16 June sailed with nearly thirty Tahitian men and women, some taken by deception.
stops.quote: The most likely source for these was Tahiti, to which Bounty returned on 6 June.

stops.text: The mutineers began building a moated enclosure called Fort George. Clashes with the islanders, mainly over property and women, ended in a pitched battle in which 66 islanders were killed. Sixteen of the party then chose to return to Tahiti.
stops.quote: There were persistent clashes with the native population, mainly over property and women, culminating in a pitched battle in which 66 islanders were killed and many wounded.

stops.text: Christian landed 15 of the 16 men who had voted to stay. That evening he cut the anchor rope and sailed with the Tahitians who were aboard, mainly women. He put six elderly women ashore on Mo'orea and kept 20 Polynesians, 14 of them women.
stops.quote: That evening, Christian coaxed aboard Bounty a party of Tahitians, mainly women, for a social gathering.

stops.text: After months of searching, Christian found Pitcairn, uninhabited and almost inaccessible, 188 nautical miles east of its recorded position. The ship was stripped and burned on 23 January. Christian settled with Mauatua, and a son was born.
stops.quote: After months of searching, Christian rediscovered the island on 15 January 1790, 188 nautical miles (348 km; 216 mi) east of its recorded position.

stops.text: Tensions grew over the mutineers treating the Tahitians, especially the women, as their property. Tahitians killed several mutineers in a series of murders. By 1794 the six Tahitian men were all dead, killed by the mutineers' widows or by each other.
stops.quote: In September 1793 matters degenerated into extreme violence, when several of the mutineers—possibly including Christian, Williams, Martin, Mills, and Brown—were killed by Tahitians in a series of murders.

notes: Legs: Bligh's boat (Tofua to Kupang) and Christian's way (Tubuai to Pitcairn) both start after the mutiny; Christian's May 1789 date at Tubuai is earlier than Bligh's Kupang arrival, but legs are told one after the other. Mutiny stop is at sea 30 nm south of Tofua, wp Tofua is the nearest island (same point as the next stop). Bligh's Tofua stop: article gives the attack on 2 May four days after landing (landing about 28 April); Norton's death is in the following sentences, not the quote. Left out: Cape Horn (never reached), Fiji, Great Barrier Reef details, Mo'orea (named only for where six women were put ashore, no events), Batavia and the Pandora mission (separate story). Tubuai and Tahiti appear twice because the ship came back. Second Tubuai stop has date 'June 1789' (the article gives 16 June for the sailing back and 'two months' there). Second Pitcairn stop is the same place later; article: Adams and a Tahitian woman, Teehuteatuaonoa, claimed Christian died in the killings, inconsistently; his grave is not found. Tahitian wording: 'Tahitian chiefs' as the article has them; Mauatua is the Polynesian woman Christian named 'Isabella'. 'Bounty Bay' not used as it is not named as a stop. Years for 1788 stops follow from the narrative.
